I urge readers not to pass any misunderstood content; if you have questions or are uncertain about something, feel free to ask the Lojban community, which can be found in #lojban on the Freenode IRC network. They will be happy to help.<br /><br />In this tutorial, Lojban text is written in courier new font and sometimes encased in {curly brackets}. Answers to exercises are colored light grey.  sleading, in which case they are worse than useless. The concept is very close to what we call a proposition in English. A bridi is a claim that some objects stand in a relation to each other, or that an object has some property. This stands in contrast to jufra, which are merely Lojban utterances, which can be bridi or anything else being said. The difference between a bridi and a jufra is that a jufra does not necessarily state anything, while a bridi does. Thus, a bridi might be true or false, while not all jufra can be said to be such.<br />To have some examples (in English, to begin with), âMozart was the greatest musician of all timeâ is a bridi, because it makes a claim with a truth value, and it involves an object, Mozart, and a property, being the greatest musician of all time. On the contrary, âOw! My toe!â is not a bridi, since it does not involve a relation, and thus does not state anything. Both, though, are jufra.<br />Try to identify the bridi among these English jufra:<br /><br />a)    âI hate it when you do that.â<br /><br />b)    âRuns.â<br /><br />c)    âWoah, that looks delicious!â<br /><br />d)    âGeez, not again.â<br /><br />e)    âNo, I own three carsâ<br /><br />f)     âNineteen minutes past eight.â<br /><br />g)    âThis Saturday, yes.â<br /><br />Answer: a, c and e are bridi. b contains no objects and the rest contain no relation or claim of a property.<br /><br />Put in Lojban terms, a bridi consists of one selbri, and one or more sumti. The selbri is the relation or claim about the object, and the sumti are the objects which are in a relation. Note that âobjectâ is not a perfect translation of âsumtiâ, since âsumtiâ can refer to not just physical !

For now, âverdicalâ in this context means that in order for a thing to qualify begin labelled as {lo klama}, it has to actually klama. This non-verdicality is perhaps over-emphasised in most many texts; The best way to describe a dog is usually to describe it as being a dog, and unless there is a good reason not to, {le gerku} is usually presumed to refer to something which is also {lo gerku}.<br />In translation, {lo gerku} is usually âa dogâ or âsome dogsâ, while {le gerku} is âthe dogâ or âthe dogsâ.  pt for one: They treat the sumti as masses instead of individuals. If there is only one object in question, these two concepts are equivalent. The difference between these two concepts lie in which selbri can be ascribed to a group of individuals versus a mass. A group of individuals can be said to fit a certain selbri, if all members of the group each fit the selbri. It is correct to describe a pack of {lo gerku}, as being black, if for each of the dogs itâs true that they are black. A mass, on the other hand, fits all the selbri which any of its members fit, as well as the selbri which none of the members fit, but which the group considered as a whole does. Thus, a mass of dogs can be both black and white. However, all the members of the mass of dogs must be dogs in order for {loi} to be applicable. Lojban Wave Lessons Continued:
by la klaku with help from la .kribacr., la xalbo and others, autumn 2011.

Chapter zero: Foreword
These lessons are an attempt to expand on the Google Wave Lessons, an excellent Lojban tutorial by kribacr, xalbo, and others, which sadly only covered the first four chapters in this tutorial. It implements the newest rules of Lojban not covered by older materials such as What is Lojban? and Lojban for Beginners.

If you are new to Lojban, I recommend listening to any recordings you can find of spoken Lojban both before and while you are taking this tutorial, in order to make yourself familiar with the sounds and words of the language, which will not be explained here. Furthermore, try to say the things you read in Lojban accent if itâs reasonably practical. This can help your pronunciation a lot.

When taking this tutorial, itâs best to pause between lessons in order to internalize what you have learnt. I have attempted to build these lessons from the bottom up and exclude any words or concepts that have not been explained in previous lessons. Once explained, they are used freely throughout the remainder of the tutorial. I urge readers not to pass any misunderstood content; if you have questions or are uncertain about something, feel free to ask the Lojban community, which can be found in #lojban on the Freenode IRC network. They will be happy to help.

In this tutorial, Lojban text is written in courier new font and sometimes encased in {curly brackets}. Answers to exercises are colored light grey. Tilt your screen or copy the text into some other medium, an address bar or text editor in order to see it.

Lastly, I have as far as possible attempted to use the Lojban words for grammatical constructs: sumkaâi instead of pro-sumti, sumtcita instead of modal and jufra instead of utterance. This is because I feel the English words are often either arbitrary, in which case they are just more words to learn, or misleading, in which case they are worse than useless. In either case, as long as the words are specific to those who are learning Lojban anyway, there is no reason for them to exist as separate English words.


Lojban Lessons â lesson one (bridi, jufra, sumti and selbri)
A bridi is the most central unit of Lojban utterances. The concept is very close to what we call a proposition in English. A bridi is a claim that some objects stand in a relation to each other, or that an object has some property. This stands in contrast to jufra, which are merely Lojban utterances, which can be bridi or anything else being said. The difference between a bridi and a jufra is that a jufra does not necessarily state anything, while a bridi does. Thus, a bridi might be true or false, while not all jufra can be said to be such.
To have some examples (in English, to begin with), âMozart was the greatest musician of all timeâ is a bridi, because it makes a claim with a truth value, and it involves an object, Mozart, and a property, being the greatest musician of all time. On the contrary, âOw! My toe!â is not a bridi, since it does not involve a relation, and thus does not state anything. Both, though, are jufra.
Try to identify the bridi among these English jufra:

a)    âI hate it when you do that.â

b)    âRuns.â

c)    âWoah, that looks delicious!â

d)    âGeez, not again.â

e)    âNo, I own three carsâ

f)     âNineteen minutes past eight.â

g)    âThis Saturday, yes.â

Answer: a, c and e are bridi. b contains no objects and the rest contain no relation or claim of a property.

Put in Lojban terms, a bridi consists of one selbri, and one or more sumti. The selbri is the relation or claim about the object, and the sumti are the objects which are in a relation. Note that âobjectâ is not a perfect translation of âsumtiâ, since âsumtiâ can refer to not just physical objects, but can also purely abstract things like âThe idea of warfareâ. A better translation would be something like âsubject, direct or indirect objectâ for sumti, and âverbâ for selbri, though, as we will see, this is not optimal either.
We can now write the first important lesson down:
bridi = selbri + one or more sumti
Put another way, a bridi states that some sumti do/are something explained by a selbri.

Identify the sumti and selbri equivalents in these jufra:
âI will pick up my daughters with my carâ

Answer: selbri: âpick up (with)â. sumti: âIâ, âmy daughtersâ, âmy carâ

âHe bought sixteen new shirts from Lea&Levyâs for just two hundred euro!â

Answer: selbri: âbought (from) (for)â sumti: âHeâ, âsixteen new shirtsâ, âLea&Lewisâ and âtwo hundred eurosâ

Since these concepts are so fundamental to Lojban, letâs have a third example: âSo far, the EPA have done nothing about the amount of sulphur dioxide in the air.â

Answer: selbri: âhave done (about)â sumti: âThe EPAâ, ânothingâ and âthe amount of sulphor dioxide in the airâ

Now try begin making Lojban bridi. For this you will need to use some word, which can act as selbri:
dunda x1 gives x2 to x3 (without payment)
pelxu x1 is yellow
zdani x1 is a home of x2

Notice that these words meaning âgiveâ, âyellowâ and âhomeâ would be considered a verb, an adjective and a noun in English. In Lojban, there are no such categories and no such distinction. dunda can be translated âgivesâ (verb), âis a giverâ (noun), âis givingâ (adjective) as well as to an adverb form. They all act as selbri, and are used in the same way.

As well as a few words, which can act as sumti:
mi âIâ or âWeâ â the one or those who are speaking.
ti âthisâ â a close thing or event nearby which can be pointed to by the speaker.
do âyouâ â the one or those who are being spoken to.

See the strange translations of the selbri above - especially the x1, x2 and x3? Those are called sumti places. They are places where sumti can go to fill a bridi. Filling a sumti in a place states that the sumti fits in that place. The second place of dunda, for example, x2, is the thing being given. The third is the object which receives the thing. Notice also that the translation of dunda has the word âtoâ in it. This is because, while this word is needed in English to signify the receiver, the receiver is in the third sumti place of dunda. So when you fill the third sumti place of dunda, the sumti you fill in is always the receiver, and you donât need an equivalent to the word âtoâ!

To say a bridi, you simply say the x1 sumti first, then the selbri, then any other sumti.
Usual bridi: [x1 sumti] [selbri] [x2 sumti] [x3 sumti] [x4 sumti] [x5 sumti] [and so on]
The order can be played around with, but for now, we stick with the usual form. To say âI give this to youâ you just say mi dunda ti do, with the three sumti at the right places.

So, how would you say âThis is a home of meâ?

Answer: ti zdani mi

Try a few more in order to get the idea of a place structure sink in.

âYou give this to meâ?

Answer:  do dunda ti mi

And translate ti pelxu

Answer: âThis is yellow.â

Quite easy once you get the hang of it, right?

Multiple bridi after each other are separated by .i This is the Lojban equivalent of full stop, but it usually goes before bridi instead of after them. Itâs often left out before the first bridi, though, as in all these examples:

ti zdani mi  .i ti pelxu âThis is a home to me. This is yellow.â

Before you move on to the next lesson, I recommend that you take a break for at least seven minutes to let the information sink in.


Lojban Lessons â lesson two (FA and zoâe)
Most selbri have from one to five sumti places, but some have more. Here is a selbri with four sumti places:
vecnu x1 sells x2 to x3 for price x4

If I want to say âI sell thisâ, it would be undesirable to fill the sumti places x3 and x4, which specify who I sell the thing to, and for what price. Luckily, I donât need to. sumti places can be filled with zoâe. zoâe indicates to us that the value of the sumti place is unspecified because itâs unimportant or can be determined from context.
zoâe âsomethingâ Fills a sumti place with something, but does not state what.

So to say âI sell to youâ, I could say mi vecnu zoâe do zoâe â I sell something to you for some price.
How would you say: âThatâs a home (for somebody)â?

Answer: ti zdani zoâe

How about â(someone) gives this to (someone)â?

Answer: zoâe dunda ti zoâe

Still, filling out three zoâe just to say that a thing is being sold takes time. Therefore you donât need to write all the zoâe in a bridi. The rule simply is that if you leave out any sumti, they will be considered as if they contained zoâe. If the bridi begins with a selbri, the x1 is presumed to be omitted and the x1 becomes zoâe.
Try it out. Whatâs Lojban for âI sellâ?

Answer: mi vecnu

And what does zdani mi mean?

Answer: âSomething is a home of meâ or just âI have a home.â

As mentioned earlier, the form doesnât have to be [x1 sumti] [selbri] [x2 sumti] [x3 sumti] (ect.) In fact, you can place the selbri anywhere you want, just not at the beginning of the bridi. If you do that, the x1 is considered left out and filled with zoâe instead. So the following three jufra are all the exactly same bridi:
mi dunda ti do
mi ti dunda do
mi ti do dunda

Sometimes this is used for poetic effect. âYou sell yourselfâ could be do do vecnu, which sounds better than do vecnu do. Or it can be used for clarity if the selbri is very long and therefore better be left at the end of the bridi.

There are also several ways to play around with the order of the sumti inside the bridi. The most easy one is by using the words fa, fe, fi, fo and fu. Notice that the vowels are the five vowels in the Lojban alphabet in order. Using one of these words marks that the next sumti will fill the x1, x2, x3, x4 and x5 respectively. The next sumti after that will be presumed to fill a slot one greater than the previous. To use an example:
dunda fa do fe ti do â âGiving by you of this thing to youâ. fa marks the x1, the giver, which is you. fe marks the thing being given, the x2. Sumti counting then continues from fe, meaning that the last sumti fills x3, the object receiving.

Attempt to translate the following three sentences:

mi vecnu fo ti fe do

Answer: âI sell, for the price of this, youâ. or âI sell you for the price of thisâ (probably pointing to a bunch of money)

zdani fe ti

Answer: âThis has a homeâ. Here, the fe is redundant.

vecnu zoâe mi ti fa do

Answer: âYou sell something to me for this priceâ


Lojban Lessons â lesson three (tanru and lo)
In this chapter, you will become familiar with the concept of tanru. A tanru is formed when a brivla is put in front of another brivla, modifying itâs meaning. A tanru is itself a selbri, and can combine with other brivla or tanru to form more complex tanru. Thus zdani vecnu is a tanru, as well as  pelxu zdani vecnu, which is made from the tanru pelxu zdani and the single brivla word vecnu. To understand the concept of tanru, consider the English noun combination âlemon treeâ. If you didnât know what a lemon tree was, but had heard about both lemons and trees, you would not be able to deduce what a lemon tree was. Perhaps a lemon-colored tree, or a tree shaped like a lemon, or a tree whose bark tastes like lemon. The only things you could know for sure would be that it would be a tree, and it would be lemon-like in some way.
A tanru is closely analogous to this. It cannot be said exactly what a zdani vecnu is, but it can be said that it is definitely a vecnu, and that itâs zdani-like in some way. And it could be zdani-like in any way. In theory, no matter how silly or absurd the connection to zdani was, it could still truly be a zdani vecnu. However, it must actually be a vecnu in the ordinary sense in order for the tanru to apply. You could gloss zdani vecnu as âhouse sellerâ, or even better but worse sounding âa home-type-of sellerâ. The place structure of a tanru is always that of the rightmost selbri. Itâs also said that the left selbri modifies the right selbri.
âReally?â, you ask, sceptically, âIt doesnât matter how silly the connection to the left word in a tanru is, itâs still true? So I could call all sellers for zdani vecnu and then make up some silly excuse why I think itâs zdani-like?â
Well yes, but then youâd be a dick. Or at least youâd be intentionally misleading. In general, you should use a tanru when itâs obvious how the left word relates to the right.

Attempt to translate the following: ti pelxu zdani do

Answer: âThat is a yellow home for youâ Again, we donât know in which way itâs yellow. Probably itâs painted yellow, but we donât know for sure.

mi vecnu dunda

Answer: âI sell-like giveâ. What can that mean? No idea. It certainly doesnât mean that you sold something, since, by definition of dunda, there can be no payment involved. It has to be a giveaway, but be sell-like in some aspect.

â¦ And now for something completely different. What if I wanted to say I sold to a German?
dotco x1 is German/reflects German culture in aspect x2

I canât say mi vecnu zoâe dotco because that would leave two selbri in a bridi, which is not permitted. I could say mi dotco vecnu but that would be unnecessary vague - I could sell in a German way.. Likewise, if I want to say âI am friends with an Americanâ, what should I say?
pendo â 1x is a friend of x2
merko â x1 is American/reflect US culture in aspect x2

Again, the obvious would be to say mi pendo merko, but that would for a tanru, meaning âI am friend-like Americanâ, which is wrong. What we really want to is to take the selbri merko and transform it into a sumti so it can be used in the selbri pendo. This is done by the two words lo and ku.
lo â generic begin convert selbri to sumti word. Extracts x1 of selbri to use as sumti.
ku â end convert selbri to sumti process.

You simply place a selbri between these two words, and it takes anything that can fill the x1 of that selbri and turns it into a sumti.
So for instance, the things that can fill zdaniâs x1are only things which are homes of somebody. So lo zdani ku means âa or some homes for somebody.â Similarly, if I say that something is pelxu, it means itâs yellow. So lo pelxu ku refers to something yellow.

Now you got the necessary grammar to be able to say âI am friends with an American.â How?

Answer: mi pendo lo merko ku

There is a good reason why the ku is necessary. Try to translate âA German sells this to meâ

Answer: lo dotco ku vecnu ti mi If you leave out the ku, you do not get a bridi, but simply three sumti. Since loâ¦ku cannot convert bridi, the ti is forced outside the sumti, the lo-construct is forced to close and it simply becomes the three sumti of lo dotco vecnu [ku], ti and mi.

You always have to be careful with jufra like lo zdani ku pelxu. If the ku is left out the conversion process does not end, and it simply becomes one sumti, made from the tanru zdani pelxu and then converted with lo.


Lojban Lessons â lesson four (attitudinals)
Another concept which can be unfamiliar to English speaker is that of attitudinals, which  are words which express emotions directly. The idea of attitudinals originated in the feminist constructed language LÃ¡adan, supposedly to enable true female emotions. The idea was that female emotional expression was hindered by male dominated language.
In Lojban, there is no such agenda, and attitudinals most probably have been designed into the language because they turned out to be incredibly awesome and useful. They all have a so-called free grammar, which means that they can appear almost anywhere within bridi without disrupting the bridiâs grammar or any grammatical constructs.
In Lojban grammar, an attitudinal applies to the previous word. If that previous word is a word which begins a construct (like .i or lo), it applies to the entire construct. Likewise, if the attitudinal follows a word which ends a construct like ku, it applies to the ended construct.

Letâs have two attitudinals to make some examples:
.ui: attitudinal: simple pure emotion: happiness - unhappiness
zaâa: attitudinal: evidential: I directly observe

Note that in the definition of .ui, there are listed two emotions, happiness and unhappiness. This means that .ui is defined as happiness, while its ânegationâ, means unhappiness. âNegationâ might be the wrong word here. Technically, the other definition of .ui is another construct, .ui nai. Most of the time, the second definition of attitudinals - the ones suffixed with nai - really is the negation of the bare attitudinal. Other times, not so much.

And some more selbri, just for the heck of it:
citka â x1 eats x2
plise â x1 is an apple of strain/type x2

The sentence do citka lo plise ku .ui, means âYou eat an apple, yay!â (expressing especially that it is the apple that the speaker is happy about, not the eating, or the fact that it was you.) In the sentence do zaâa citka lo plise ku, the speaker directly observes that it is indeed âyouâ, who eats an apple as opposed to someone else.

If an attitudinal is placed at the beginning of the bridi, it is understood to apply to an explicit or implicit .i, thus applying to the entire bridi:
.ui zaâa do dunda lo plise ku mi â âYay, I observe that you give an/some apple to me!â

mi vecnu .ui nai lo zdani âI sell (which sucks!) a houseâ.

Try it out with a few examples. First, though, here are some more attitudinals:
.uâu attitudinal: simple pure emotion: guilt - remorselessness - innocence.
.oi attitudinal: complex pure emotion: pain - complacency - comfort.
.iu attitudinal: miscellaneous pure emotion: love - hate.

Look at that, two words with three emotions in the definition! The middle one is accessed by suffixinng with cuâi. Itâs considered the midpoint of the emotion.

Try saying âI give something to a German, who I loveâ

Answer: mi dunda fi lo dotco ku .iu or zoâe instead of fi

Now âAah, I eat a yellow appleâ

Answer: .oi nai mi citka lo pelxu plise ku

Letâs have another attitudinal of a different kind to illustrate something peculiar:
.ei Attitudinal: complex propositional emotion: obligation - freedom.

So, quite easy: âI have to give the apple awayâ is mi dunda .ei lo plise ku, right? It is, actually! When you think about it, thatâs weird. Why is it that all the other attitudinals we have seen so far expresses the speakers feeling about the bridi, but this one actually changes what the bridi means? Surely, by saying âI have to give the apple awayâ, we say nothing about whether the apple actually is being given away. If I had used .ui, however, I would actually have stated that I gave the apple away, and that I was happy about it. Whatâs that all about?

This issue, exactly how attitudinals change the conditions on which a bridi is true, is a subject of a minor debate. The official, âtextbookâ rules, which probably wonât be changed, is that there is a distinction between âpure emotionsâ and âpropositional emotionsâ. Only propostional emotions can change the truth conditions, while pure emotions cannot. In order to express a propositional emotional attitudinal without changing the truth value of the bridi, you can just separate it fro the bridi with .i. There is also a word for explicitly conserving or changing the truth conditions of a bridi:
daâi attitudinal: discursive: supposing - in fact
Saying daâi in a bridi changes the truth conditions. Saying daâi nai preserves it, even with a propositional emotional attitudinal.

So, whatâs two ways of saying âI give the apple away, to which I feel obligationâ?

Answer: mi dunda lo plise .i .ei  and mi dunda daâi nai .ei lo plise

The feeling of an attitudinal can be subscribed to someone else using dai. Usually in ordinary speech, the attitudinal is subscribed to the listener, but it doesnât have to be so. Also, because the word is glossed âempathyâ (feeling others emotions), some Lojbanists mistakenly think that the listener must share the emotion being subscribed to others.
Example: uâi .oi dai citka ti - âHa ha, this was eaten! That must have hurt!â

What often used phrase could .oi uâi dai mean?

Answer: âOuch, very funny.â

And another one to test your knowledge: Try to translate âHe was sorry he sold a houseâ (remembering, that tense is implied and need not be specified. Also, âheâ could be obvious from context)

Answer: uâu dai vecnu lo zdani ku

Lastly, the intensity of an attitudinal can be specified using certain words. These can be used after an attitudinal, or an attitudinal with nai or cuâi suffixed. Itâs less clear what happens when you attach it to other words, like a selbri, must itâs mostly understood as intensifying or weakening the selbri in some unspecified way:
modifying word	intensity
cai	extreme/maximal
sai	strong
(none)	unspecified (usually medium)
ruâe	weak


What emotion is expressed using .uâi nai sai ?

Answer: Strong weariness

And how would you express that you are mildly remorseless?

Answer: .uâu cuâi ruâe

Lojban lessons â lesson five (SE)
Before we venture into the territory of more complex constructs, you should learn another mechanism for reordering the sumti of a selbri. This, as we will show, is very useful for making description-like sumti (the kind of sumti with lo).
Consider the sentence âI eat a giftâ, which might be appropriate if that gift is an apple. To translate this, it would seem natural to look up a selbri meaning âgiftâ before continuing. However, if one looks carefully at the definition of dunda, x1 gives x2 to x3, one realizes that the x2 of dunda is something given â a gift.
So, to express that sentence, we canât say mi citka lo dunda ku, because lo dunda ku would be the x1 of dunda, which is a donor of a gift. Cannibalism aside, we donât want to say that. What we want is a way to extract the x2 of a selbri.
This is one example where it is useful to use the word se. What se does is to modify a selbri such that the x1 and x2 of that selbri trade places. The construct of se + selbri is on its own considered one selbri. Letâs try with an ordinary sentence:
fanva = âx1 translates x2 to language x3 from language x4 with result of translation x5â
ti se fanva mi = mi fanva ti
This is translated by me (= I translate this). Often, but not always, bridi with se-constructs are translated to sentences with the passive voice, since the x1 is often the object taking action.
se has its own family of words. All of them swap a different place with the x1.
se	swap x1 and x2
te	swap x1 and x3
ve	swap x1 and x4
xe	swap x1 and x5


Note that s, t, v, and x are consecutive consonants in the lojban alphabet.

So: Using this knowledge, what would ti xe fanva ti mean?

Answer: âThis is a translation of thisâ (or fanva ti fu ti)

se and its family can of course be combined with fa and its family. The result can be very confusing indeed, if you wish to make it so:
klama = âx1 travels/goes to x2 from x3 via x4 using x5 as transportation deviceâ
fu lo zdani ku te klama fe do ti fa mi. = mi te klama do ti lo zdani ku and since te exchanges x1 and x3: = ti klama do mi lo zdani ku
âThis travels to you from me via a home.â Of course, no one would make such a sentence except to confuse people, or cruelly to test their understanding of Lojban grammar.
And thus, we have come to the point where we can say âI eat a gift.â. Simply exchange the sumti places of dunda to get the gift to be x1, then extract this new x1 with lo...ku. So, how would you say it?
One (possible) answer: mi citka lo se dunda ku
This shows one of the many uses for se and its family.


Lojban lessons â lesson six (NU)
So far we have only expressed single sentences one at a time. To express more complex things, however, you often need subordinate sentences. Luckily, these are much easier in Lojban than what one would expect.
We can begin with an example to demonstrate this: âI am happy that you are my friend.â Here, the main bridi is âI am happy that X.â, and the sub-bridi is âYou are my friend.â Looking at the definition for âhappyâ, which is gleki:
gleki = âx1 is happy about x2 (event/state)â
One sees that the x2 needs to be an event or a state. This is natural, because one cannot be happy about an object in itself, only about some state the object is in. But alas! Only bridi can express a state or an event, and only sumti can fill the x2 of gleki!.
As you might have guessed, there is a solution. The words suâu...kei is a generic âconvert bridi to selbriâ function, and works just like loâ¦ku. Example:
mrobiâo âx1 dies under condition x2â
mi suâu do mrobiâo kei â âI am your deathâ.
Itâs hard to find good uses of a bridi as a selbri, and the above example seems a little unconvincing. However, since suâu BRIDI kei is a selbri, one can convert it to a sumti using lo...ku.
Now we have the equipment to express âI am happy that you are my friendâ. Try it out!
pendo âx1 is a friend of x2â

Answer: mi gleki lo suâu do pendo mi kei ku

However, suâuâ¦kei does not see much use. People prefer to use the more specific words nuâ¦kei and duâuâ¦kei. They work the same way, but mean something different. nuâ¦kei treats the bridi in between as an event or state, and duâuâ¦kei treats it as an abstract bridi, for expressing things like ideas, thoughts or truths. All these words (except kei) are called abstractors. There are many of them, and only few are used much. suâuâ¦kei is a general abstractor, and will work in all cases.

Use nu to say âIâm happy about talking to you.â
tavla x1 talks to x2 about subject x3 in language x4.

Answer: mi gleki lo nu tavla do (notice both the English and the Lojban is vague as to who is doing the talking).
Other important abstractors include: ka...kei (property abstraction), siâo...kei (concept/idea abstraction), ni...kei (quantity abstraction) among others.

It is important to notice that some abstractors have several sumti places. As an example, duâu can be mentioned. duâu is defined:
duâu = âabstractor. x1 is the predicate/bridi of [bridi] expressed in sentence x2â.
The other sumti places besides x1 is rarely used, but lo se duâu BRIDI kei ku is sometimes used as a sumti for indirect quotation: âI said that I was given a dogâ can be written mi cusku lo se duâu mi te dunda lo gerku ku kei ku, if you will pardon the weird example.
cusku x1 expresses x2 to x3 through medium x4

Lojban lessons â lesson seven (NOI)
While weâre at it, thereâs another type of subordinate bridi. These are called relative clauses. They are sentences which add some description to a sumti. Indeed, the âwhichâ in the previous sentence marked the beginning of a relative clause in English describing relative clauses. In Lojban, they come in two flavors, and it might be worth distinguishing the two kinds before learning how to express them.
The two kinds are called restrictive and non-restrictive (or incidential) relative clauses. An example would be good here:
âMy brother, who is two meters tall, is a politician.â This can be understood in two ways. I could have several brothers, in which case saying he is two meters tall will let you know which brother I am talking about. Or I might have only one brother, in which case I am simply giving you additional information.

In English as well as Lojban we distinguish between these two kinds â the first interpretation is restrictive (since it helps restrict the possible brothers I might be talking about), the second non-restrictive. When speaking English, context and tone of voice (or in written English, punctuation) helps us distinguish between these two, but not so in Lojban. Lojban use the constructs poiâ¦kuâo and noiâ¦kuâo for restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses, respectively.
Letâs have a Lojbanic example, which can also explain our strange gift-eating behaviour in the example in chapter 5:

mi citka lo se dunda ku poi plise kuâo = âI eat a gift such that (something is) an appleâ. Here the poiâ¦kuâo is placed just after lo se dunda ku, so it applies to the gift. To be strict, the relative clause does not specify what is an apple, but since the relative clause applies to the gift, we can safely assume that is means the gift is an apple. After all, in the context of chapter 5, this seems reasonable. If we want to be absolutely sure that it indeed was the gift that was an apple, we use the word keâa, which is a pro-sumti (a Lojban pronoun) representing the sumti which the relative clause is attached to.
.ui mi citka lo se dunda ku poi keâa plise kuâo = âYay, I eat a gift, which is an appleâ.
To underline the difference between restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses, hereâs another example:
lojbo = âx1 reflects Lojbanic culture/community is aspect x2; x1 is Lojbanic.â
mi noi lojbo kuâo fanva fo lo lojbo ku = âI, who am a Lojbanic, translate from some Lojbanic language.â Here, there is not multiple things which mi could refer to, and the fact that I am lojbanic is merely additional information not needed to identify me. Therefore noiâ¦kuâo is appropriate.
See if you can translate this: âI flirt with a man who is beautiful/handsomeâ.
nanmu âx1 is a manâ
melbi âx1 is beautiful to x2 in aspect (ka) x3 by standard x4â
cinjikca âx1 flirts/courts x2, exhibiting sexuality x3 by standard x4â
Answer: mi cinjikca lo nanmu ku poi (keâa) melbi kuâo

On a more technical side note, it might be useful to know that lo SELBRI ku is officially defined as zoâe noi keâa SELBRI kuâo.


Lojban Lessons â Lesson eight (terminator elision)
.au daâi mi djica lo nu le merko poi tunba mi vau ku'o ku jimpe lo du'u mi na nelci lo nu voâa darxi mi vau kei ku vau kei ku vau kei ku vau
 -  âI wish the American, who is my sibling, would understand that I donât like that he hits me.â
Regardless of whether the above sentence is being understood, (it shouldnât, as it contains words we have not covered in these lessons yet) one thing stands out: As more complex Lojban structures are learned, more and more of the sentences get filled with ku, kei, kuâo and other of those words which by themselves carry no meaning.

The function of all these words are to signal the end of a certain grammatical construct, like for instance âconvert selbri to sumtiâ in the case of loâ¦ku. The English word for this kind of word is âterminatorâ, the Lojban word is faâormaâo. They are colored grey in the example above.
Note: The vau in the above example are the terminator for âend bridiâ. There is a good reason you have not yet seen it, stay tuned.

In most spoken and written Lojban, most terminators are skipped (elided). This greatly saves syllables in speech and space in writing, however, one must always be careful when eliding terminators. In the simple example lo merko ku klama, removing the terminator ku would yield lo merko klama, which is a single sumti made from the tanru merko klama. Thus, it means âan American travelerâ instead of âan American travelsâ. Terminator elision can lead to very wrong results if done incorrectly, which is why you havenât learned about it until now.

The rule for when terminators can be elided is very simple, at least in theory: âYou can elide a terminator, if and only if doing so does not change the grammatical constructs in the sentence.â
Most terminators can be safely elided at the end of the bridi. Exceptions are the obvious ones like âend quoteâ-terminators and âend bridi groupingâ-terminators. This is why vau is almost never used â simply beginning a new bridi with .i will always terminate the preceding bridi anyway. It has one frequent use, however. Since attitudinals always apply to the preceding word, applying it to a terminator applies it to the entire construct which is terminated. Using vau, one can then use attitudinals afterthought and apply them to the entire bridi:
zaâa do dunda lo zdani lo prenu... vau iâe - âI see that you give a home to a person... I approve!â
prenu x1 is a person; x1 has a personality.

Knowing the basic rules for terminator elision, we can thus return to the original sentence and begin removing terminators:

.au daâi mi djica lo nu le merko poi tunba mi vau ku'o ku jimpe lo du'u mi na nelci lo nu voâa darxi mi vau kei ku vau kei ku vau kei ku vau

Removing the first three terminators will leave both tunba and jimpe as selbri inside the relative clause. Since this is not grammatical (only one bridi can be in a relative clause, and only one selbri in one bridi), eliding them will still leave jimpe outside the relative clause. Nor can it make a tanru with merko, since that word already had a relative clause attached to it, which only sumti can have. That means we can deduce that removing those three are safe. Furthermore, all the terminators at the very end can be elided too, since beginning a new bridi will terminate all of these constructs anyway.
We then end up with:
.au daâi mi djica lo nu le merko poi tunba mi jimpe lo du'u mi na nelci lo nu voâa darxi mi â with no terminators at all!

When eliding terminators, it is a good idea to be acquainted with cu. cu is one of those words which can make your (Lojbanic) life a lot easier. What it does is to separate any previous sumti from the selbri. One could say that it defines the next word to be a selbri, and terminates exactly as much as it needs to in order to do that.

prami = âx1 loves x2â

lo suâu do cusku lo se duâu do prami mi vau kei ku vau kei ku se djica mi =
lo suâu do cusku lo se duâu do prami mi cu se djica mi
âThat you say that you love me is desired by beâ or âI wish you said you loved meâ
note: cu is not a terminator, because it is not tied to one specific construct. But it can be used to elide other terminators.

One of the greatest strengths of cu is that it quickly becomes easy to intuitively understand. By itself it means nothing, but it reveals the structure of Lojban expressions by identifying the core selbri. In the original example with the violent American brother, using cu before jimpe does not change the meaning of the sentence in any way, but might make it easier to read.

In the following couple of chapters, cu will be used when necessary, and all terminators elided if possible. The elided terminators will be encased in square brackets, as shown below. Try to translate it!
du âx1 equals/is the same as x2, x3, x4, x5, x6 (and so on)â
vajni âx1 is important to x2 for reason x3â
jimpe âx1 understands that x2 (duâu-abstraction) is true about x3â
aâo - Attitudinal: Hope - despair

aâo do noi keâa lojbo .iâe [kuâo] [ku] cu jimpe lo duâu lo faâormaâo [ku] cu vajni [vau] [kei] [ku] [vau]
What do I state?

Answer: âI hope that you, a proud Lojbanist, understands that terminators are importantâ

Fun side note: Most people well-versed in terminator elision do it so instinctively that they often must be reminded how important understanding terminators are to the understanding of Lojban. Therefore, each Tuesday have been designated âTerminator Dayâ or faâormaâo djedi on the Lojban IRC chatroom. During Terminator Day, many people try (and often fail) to remember writing out all terminators with some very verbose conversations as a result.


Lojban Lessons - Lesson nine (sumtcita)

So far we have been doing pretty good with the selbri we have had at hand. However, there is a finite amount of selbri out there, and in many cases the sumti places are not useful for what we had in mind. What if, say, i want to say that I am translating using a computer? There is no place in the structure of fanva to specify what tool I translate with, since most of the time, that is not necessary. Not to worry, this chapter is on how to add additional sumti places to the selbri.

The most basic way to add sumti places are with fiâo...feâu (yes, another example of a terminator, feâu. Itâs almost never necessary, so this might be the last time you ever see it.)
In between these two words goes a selbri, and like lo...ku, fiâo...feâu extracts the x1 of the selbri put into it. However, with fiâo...feâu, the selbri place is converted, not to a sumti, but to a sumtcita, meaning âsumti-labelâ, with the place structure of the x1 of the selbri it converted. This sumtcita then absorbs the next sumti. One could say that using a sumtcita, you import a sumti place from another selbri, and add it to the bridi being said.
Note: Sometimes, especially in older texts, the term âtagâ or âmodalâ is used for sumtcita. Ignore those puny English expressions. We teach proper Lojban here.

While it is hard to grasp the process from reading about it, an example can perhaps show its actual simplicity:
skami âx1 is a computer for purpose x2â
pilno âx1 uses x2 as a tool for doing x3â

mi fanva ti fiâo se pilno [feâu] lo skami [ku][vau].- âI translate this with a computerâ The x2 of pilno, which is the x1 of se pilno is a place structure for a tool being used by someone. This place structure is captured by fiâo...feâu, and then filled by lo skami. The idea of sumtcita is sometimes expressed in English using the following translation:
âI translate this with-tool: a computerâ

A sumtcita can only absorb one sumti, which is always the following one. Alternatively, the sumtcita construct can be terminated with ku, in which case a zoâe is implied to fill the sumtcita. Or, one could imagine an elided sumti being terminated with the ku.
zukte âx1 is a volitional entity carrying out action x2 for purpose x3â
fiâo zukte [feâu] ku lo skami [ku] cu pilno lo lojbo [ku][vau] - âWith volition, a computer used something Lojbanicâ (perhaps implying that a Lojbanic computer went sentient? Tough it does not specify who had volition. It could just be the programmer who programmed the computer - how boring.)

What does mi jimpe fi lo lojban [ku] fiâo se tavla [feâu] mi  state?

Answer: âI understand something about Lojban, spoken to meâ

Putting the sumtcita right in front of the selbri also makes it self-terminate, since sumtcita only can absorb sumti, and not selbri. This fact will be of importance in next chapter, as you will see.

Sadly, fiâo is not used very often despite its flexibility. What IS used very often, though, are BAI. BAI are a class of Lojban words, which in themselves act as sumtcita. An example of this is zuâe, the BAI for zukte. Gramatically, zuâe is the same as fiâo zukte feâu. Thus, the above example could be reduced to:
zuâe ku lo skami [ku] cu pilno lo lojbo [ku] [vau]. There exist something like 60 BAI, and a lot of these are very useful indeed. Furtermore, BAI can also be converted with se and friends, meaning that se zuâe is equal to fiâo se zukte feâu, which results in a great deal more BAI.

Lojban Lessons - Lesson ten (PU, FAhA, ZI, VA, ZEhA, VEhA)

How unfamiliar to the English-speaker a language Lojban is when one can read through nine chapters of Lojban grammar without meeting a tense once. This is because, unlike many natural languages (most Indo-European ones, for instance), all tenses in Lojban are optional. Saying mi citka lo cirla [ku] can mean âI eat cheeseâ or âI ate the cheeseâ or âI always eat cheeseâ or âIn a moment, i will have just finished eating cheeseâ. Context resolves what is correct, and in most conversation, tenses are not needed at all. However, when itâs needed itâs needed, and it must be taught.
Like many other languages, the Lojban tense system is perhaps the most difficult part of the language. Unlike many other languages though, itâs perfectly regular and makes sense. So fear not, for it will not involve sweating to learn how to modify the selbri or anything silly like that.
Furthermore, Lojban tenses are unusual because they treat time and space fundamentally the same - saying that i worked a long time ago is not grammatically different than saying i work far away to the north.

No, in the Lojban tense system, all tenses are sumtcita, which we have conveniently just made ourselves familiar with. There are many different kinds of tense-sumtcita, so letâs start at the ones most familiar to English-speakers.
{pu} - sumtcita: before [sumti]
{ca} - sumtcita: at the same time as [sumti]
{ba} - sumtcita: after [sumti]

These are like the English concepts âbeforeâ, ânowâ and âafterâ. In actuality though, one could argue that two point-like events can never occur exactly simultaneously, rendering {ca} useless. But {ca} extends slightly into the past and the future, meaning just âabout nowâ. This is because human beings donât perceive time in a perfectly logical way, and the Lojban tense system reflects that.

Side note: It was actually suggested making the Lojban tense system relativistic. That idea, however, was dropped, because it is counter-intuitive, and would mean that to learn Lojban, one would have to learn the theory of relativity first.  

So, how would you say âI express this after I came here?â (pointing to a paper)

Answer: mi cusku ti ba lo nu mi klama ti [vau] [kei [ku] [vau]

Usually when speaking, we do not need to specify which event this action is in the past relative to. In: âI gave a computer awayâ, we can assume that the action happened relative to ânowâ, and thus we can elide the sumti of the sumtcita, because itâs obvious:
{pu ku mi dunda lo skami [ku] [vau]} or
{mi dunda lo skami [ku] pu [ku] [vau]} or, more commonly
{mi pu [ku] dunda lo skami [ku] [vau]}. The sumti which fills the sumtcita is an implied {zoâe}, which is almost always understood as relative to the speakers time and place (this is especially important when speaking about left and right). If speaking about some events that happened some other time than the present, it is sometimes assumed that all tenses are relative to that event which is being spoken about. In order to clarify that all tenses are relative to the speakers current position, the word {nau} can be used at any time. Another word, {ki} marks a tense which is then considered the new standard. That will be taught way later.

{gugde} = âx1 is the country of people x2 with land/territory x3â

Also note that {mi pu [ku] klama lo merko gugde [ku] [vau]}, âI went to Americaâ, does not imply that Iâm not still traveling to USA, only that it was also true some time in the past, for instance five minutes ago.

As mentioned, spacial and temporal time tenses are very much alike. Contrast the previous three time tenses with these four spacial tenses:
{zuâa} sumtcita: left of [sumti]
{caâu} sumtcita: in front of [sumti]
{riâu} sumtcita: right of [sumti]
{buâu} sumtcita: at the same place as [sumti] (spacial equivalent of {ca})

{oâo}: attitudinal: patience - tolerance - anger

What would {.oâonai riâu [ku] nu lo prenu [ku] cu darxi lo gerku pu [ku] [ku] [vau] [kei] [vau]} mean? (notice the first elided ku!)

Answer: â[anger!] To the right (of something, probably me) and in the past (of some event), something is an event of a person beating a dog.â or âA man hit a dog to my right!â

If there are several tense sumtcita in one bridi, the rule is that you read them from left to right, thinking it as a so called âimaginary journeyâ, Where you begin at an implied point in time and space (default: the speakerâs now and here), and then follow the sumtcita one at a time from left to right.
Example
{mi pu [ku] ba [ku] jimpe fi lo lojbo faâormaâo [ku] [vau]} = âAt some time in the past, I will be about to know about terminators.â
{mi ba [ku] pu [ku] jimpe fi lo lojbo faâormaâo [ku] [vau]} âAt some point in the future, I will have understood about terminators.â
Since we do not specify the amount of time we move back or forth, the understanding could in both cases happen in the future or the past of when the sentence is being said.

Also, if spacial and temporal tenses are mixed, the rule is to always put temporal before spacial. If this rule is violated, it can sometimes result in syntactical ambiguity, which Lojban does not tolerate.

Suppose we want to specify that the a man hit a dog just a minute ago. The words {zi}, {za} and {zu} specifies a short, unspecified (presumably medium) and long distance in time. Notice the vowel order {i}, {a} and {u}. This order appears again and again in Lojban, and might be worth to memorize. âShortâ and âlongâ in are always context dependent, relative and subjective. Two hundred years is a short time for a species to evolve, but a long time to wait for the bus.

Similarly, spacial distance is marked by {vi}, {va} and {vu} for short, unspecified (medium) and long distance in space.
{gunka} âx1 works at x2 with objective x3â

Translate: {ba [ku] za ku mi vu [ku] gunka [vau]}

Answer: âSome time in the future, I will work a place long awayâ
Note: People rarely uses zi, za or zu without a pu or ba in front of it. This is because we always need to specify past or future in English. When you think about it Lojbanically, most of the time the time-direction is obvious, and the pu or ba superfluous!

The order in which direction-sumtcita and distance-sumtcita are said makes a difference. Remember that the meaning of several tense words are pictured by an imaginary journey reading from left to right. Thus {pu zu} is âa long time agoâ while {zu pu} is âin the past of some point in time which is a long time toward the future or the past of nowâ. In the first example, pu shows that we begin in the past, zu then that it is a long time backwards. In the second example, zu shows that we begin at some point far away in time from now, pu then, that we move backwards from that point. Thus {pu zu} is always in the past. {zu pu} could be in the future!

As briefly implied earlier, all these constructs basically treat bridi as if they were point-like in time and space. In actuality, most events plays out over a span of time and space. In the following few paragraphs, we will learn how to specify intervals of time and space.

{zeâi} sumtcita: spanning over the short time of [sumti]
{zeâa} sumtcita: spanning over the unspecified (medium) time of [sumti]
{zeâu} sumtcita: spanning over the long time of [sumti]

{veâi} sumtcita: spanning over the short space of [sumti]
{veâa} sumtcita: spanning over the unspecified (medium) space of [sumti]
{veâu} sumtcita: spanning over the long space of [sumti]

Six words at a time, I know, but remembering the vowel sequence and the similarity of the initial letter z for temporal tenses and v for spacial tenses might help the memorizing.
{.oi} - attitudinal: pain - pleasure

Translate: {.oi dai do veâu [ku] klama lo dotco gugde [ku] zeâu [ku] [vau]}

Answer: âOuch, you spend a long time traveling a long space to Germanyâ

Though most people are not familiar with spacial tenses, these new words can open up for some pretty sweet uses. One could, for instance, translate âThatâs a big dogâ as {ti veâu [ku] gerku [vau]} Saying: âThis thing dogs for a long spaceâ makes you sound retarded in English, but well spoken in Lojban!

{zeâu} and its brothers also combine with other tenses to form compound tenses. The rule for {zeâu} and the others are that any tenses preceding it marks an endpoint of the process and any tenses coming after it marks the other endpoint relative to the first. This should be demonstrated with a couple of examples:
{.oâocuâi do citka pu [ku] zeâu [ku] ba [ku] zu [ku] [vau]} - â[tolerance] you eat beginning in the past and for a long time ending at some point far into the future of when you startedâ or âHmpf, you ate for a long timeâ. One can also contrast {do ca [ku] zeâi [ku] pu [ku] klama [vau]} with {do pu [ku] zeâi [ku] ca [ku] klama [vau]}. The first event of traveling has one endpoint in the present and extends a little towards the past, while the second event has one endpoint in the past and extends only to the present (that is, slighty into the past or future) of that endpoint.
{jmive} âx1 is alive by standard x2â

What does {.ui mi pu [ku] zi [ku] zeâu [ku] jmive [vau]} express?

Answer: â[happiness!] I live from a little into the past and a long way towards the future or past (obviously the future, in this case) of that eventâ or âI am young, and have most my life ahead of me :)â

Just to underline the similarity with spacial tenses, letâs have another example, this time with spacial tenses:
{.uâe} attitudinal: wonder - commonplace

{.uâe zaâa [ku] buâu [ku] veâu [ku] caâu [ku] zdani [vau]} - What does it mean?

Answer: â[wonder] [I observe!] Extending a long space from here to my front is a home.â or âWow, this home extending ahead is huge!â

Before we continue with this syntax-heavy tense system, i recommend spending at least ten minutes doing something which doesnât occupy your brain in order to let the information sink in. Sing a song or eat a cookie very slowly - whatever, as long as you let your mind rest.


Lojban Lessons - Lesson eleven (ZAhO)

Though we wonât go through all Lojban tense constructs for now, there is one other kind of tense that I think should be taught now. These are called âevent contoursâ, and represent a very different way of viewing tenses that we have seen so far. So letâs get to it:

Using the tenses we have learned so far, we can imagine an indefinite time line, and we then place events on that line relative to the ânowâ. With event contours, however, we view each event as a process, which has certain stages: A time before it unfolds, a time when it begins, a time when it is in process, a time when it ends, and a time after it has ended. Event contours then tells us which part of the eventâs process was happening during the time specified by the other tenses. We need a couple of tenses first:

{puâo} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi has not yet happened during [sumti]
{caâo} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is in process during [sumti]
{baâo} - sumtcita: event contour: The process of bridi has ended during [sumti]

This needs to be demonstrated by some examples. Whatâs {.ui mi puâo [ku] se zdani [vau]} mean?

Answer: âYay, Iâll begin to have a homeâ.

But hey, you ask, why not just say {.ui mi ba [ku] se zdani [vau]} and even save a syllable? Because, remember, saying that you will have a home in the future says nothing about whether you have a home now. Using {puâo}, though, you say that you are now in the past of the process of you having a home, which means that you donât have one now.
Note, by the way, that {mi ba [ku] se zdani [vau]} is similar to {mi puâo [ku] se zdani [vau]}, and likewise with {baâo} and {pu}. Why do they seem reversed? Because event contours view the present as seen from the viewpoint of the process, where as the other tenses view events seen from the present.

Often, event contours are more precise that other kind of tenses. Even more clarity is achieved by combining several tenses: {aâo mi ba[ku] zi [ku] baâo [ku] gunka [vau]} - âI hope Iâve soon finished working.â

In Lojban, we also operate with an eventâs ânatural beginningâ and its ânatural endâ. The term ânaturalâ is highly subjective in this sense, and the natural end refers to the point in the process where it should end. You can say about a late train, for instance, that its process of reaching you is now extending beyond its natural end. An undercooked, but served meal, similarly, is being eaten before that processâ natural beginning. The event contours used in these examples are as follows:

{zaâo} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is in process beyond its natural end during [sumti]
{xaâo} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is immaturely in process during [sumti]

{cidja}: âx1 is food, which is edible for x2â

Translate: {.oi do citka zaâo lo nu do baâo [ku] uâe citka zoâe noi cidja do [vau] [kuâo] [vau] [kei] [ku]}

Answer: âOy, you keep eating when you have finished, incredibly, eating something edible!â
ZAhO tenses (event contours). All tenses above the line of the event signify stages covering an amount of time. All tenses below the event line signify stages which are point-like.

All of these tenses have been describing stages of a process which takes some time (as shown on the graph above; those tenses above the event like). But many of the event contours describes point like stages in the process, like its beginning. As is true of {ca} and {buâu}, they actually extend slightly into the past and future of that point, and need not to be precise.

The two most important point-like event contours are:
{coâa} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is at its beginning during [sumti]
{coâu} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is at its ending during [sumti]

Furthermore, there is a point where the process is naturally complete, but not necessarily has ended yet:
{moâu} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is at its natural ending during [sumti]
Most of the time, though, processes actually end at their natural ending; this is what makes it natural. Trains are not usually late, and people usually retrain themselves to eat only edible food.

Since a process can be interrupted and resumed, these points have earned their own event contour also:
{deâa} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is pausing during [sumti]
{diâa} - sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is resuming during [sumti]

In fact, since {jundi} means âx1 pays attention to x2â, {deâa jundi} and {diâa jundi} are common Lojban ways of saying âBRBâ and âbackâ. One could of course also say the event contours by themselves and hope the point gets across.

Finally, one can treat an entire event, from the beginning to the end as one single point using {coâi}:
{penmi} âx1 meets x2 at location x3â
{mi pu [ku] zi [ku] coâi [ku] penmi lo dotco prenu [ku] [vau]} - âA little while ago, I was at the point in time where i met a German personâ


Lojban Lessons - Lesson twelve (orders and questions)
Phew, those two long chapters with syntax heavy Lojban gives the brain something to ponder about. Especially because itâs so different from English. So letâs turn to something a little lighter: orders and questions.

What the... sit up and focus!

Since the way to express orders in English is to leave out the subject of the clause, why did you assume that it was you I was speaking to, and not ordering myself, or expressing the obligation someone else has? Because the English language understands that orders, by their very nature, are always directed towards the listener - the âyouâ, and so the subject is not necessary.
In Lojban, eliding the subject yields {zoâe}, so that possibility is sadly not open to us. Instead, we use the word {ko}, which is the imperative form of {do}. Grammatically, itâs equivalent to {do}, but it adds a layer of semantics, since it turns every statement with {ko} in it into an order. âDo such that this sentence is true for you=ko!â For the same reason we donât need the subject in English sentences, we donât need order-words derived from any other sumti than {do}.

How could you order one to go far away for a long time (using {klama} as the only selbri?)

Answer: ko veâu zeâu klama
.i zaâa dai aâo mi ca coâu ciska lo faâormaâo .i ko jimpe vau .ui - look up ciska and work it out.

Questions in Lojban are very easy to learn, and they come in two kinds: Fill in the blank, and true/false questions. Letâs begin with the true-false question kind - thatâs pretty overcomeable, since it only involves one word, {xu}.
xu works like an attitudinal in the sense that it can go anywhere, and it applies to the preceding word (or construct). It then transforms the sentence into a question, asking whether it is true or not. In order to affirm, you simply repeat the bridi:
{xu veâu zdani do} {.i veâu zdani mi}, or you just repeat the the selbri: {zdani}.
There is an even easier way to affirm using pro-bridis, but those are a tale for another time. To answer ânoâ or âfalseâ, you simply answer with the bridi negated. That too, will be left for later, but we will return to question answering by then.

The other kind is fill in the blank. Here, you ask for the question word to be replaced for a construct, which makes the bridi correct. There are several of these words, depending on what you are asking about:
ma - sumti question
mo - selbri question
xo - number question
cuâe - tense question

As well as many others. To ask about a sumti, you then just place the question word where you want your answer: {do dunda ma mi} - asks for the x2 to be filled with a correct sumti. âYou give what to me?â The combination of sumtcita + ma is very useful indeed:
{muâi} - sumtcita: motivated by the abstraction of [sumti]

{.oi do darxi mi muâi ma} - âOy, why do you hit me?!â
Letâs try another one. This time, you translate:
{.ui dai do ca zeâu pu mo}

Answer: âYouâre happy, what have you been doing all this long time until now?â Technically, it could also ask âwhat have you been?â, but answering with {.ua nai liâa remna} (Uh, human, obviously) is just being incredibly annoying on purpose.

Since tone of voice or sentence structure does not reveal whether a sentence is a question or not, one better not miss the question word. Therefore, since people tend to focus more on words in the beginning or at the end of sentences, itâs usually worth the while to re-order the sentence so that the question words are at those places. If that is not feasable, {pau} is an attitudinal marking that the sentence is a question. Contrary, {pau nai} explicitly marks any question as being rhetorical.

While we are on the topic of questions, itâs also appropriate to mention the word {kau}, which is a marker for âindirect questionâ. Whatâs an indirect question, then? Well, take a look at the sentence: {mi djuno lo duâu ma kau zdani do} - âI know what is your home.â
{djuno} âx1 knows fact(s) x2 are true about x3 by epistemology x4â
One can think it as the answer to the question {ma zdani do}. More rarely, one can mark a non-question word with {kau}, in which case one still can imagine it as the answer to a question: {mi jimpe lo duâu dunda ti kau do} - âI know what you have been given, it is this.â


Lojban Lessons - Lesson thirteen (morphology and word classes)
Back to more syntax-heavy (and interesting) stuff.
If you havenât already, I strongly suggest you find the Lojbanic recording called Story Time with Uncle Robin, or listen to someone speak Lojban on Mumble, and then practice your pronunciation. Having an internal conversation in your head in Lojban is only good if it isnât with all the wrong sounds, and learning pronunciation from written text is hard. Therefore, this lesson will not be on the Lojban sounds, however important they might be, but a short introduction to the Lojban morphology.

What is morphology? The word is derived from Greek meaning âthe study of shapesâ, and in this context, we talk about how we make words from letters and sounds, as contrasted with syntax - how we make sentences with words. Lojban operates with different morphological word classes, which are all defined by their morphology. To make it all nice and systematic though, words with certain functions tend to be grouped by morphological classes, but exceptions may occur.
Class:	Meaning	Defined By	Typical function
Words:			
- cmevla 	name-word	Beginning and ending with pause. Last sound/letter is a consonant.	Always acts as a name.
- brivla
among these are:	bridi-word	Min. 5 letters. Among first 5 letters (excluding â â â) is a consonant cluster. Ends in vowel.	Acts as a selbri by default. Always has a place structure.
------- gismu (root word)	root-word	5 letters of the form CVCCV or CCVCV	One to five sumti places. Covers basic concepts.
------- luvjo 	compound word. Derived from from âlujvlaâ, meaning âcomplex wordâ	Min. 6 letters. Made by stringing rafsi together with binding letters if necessary.	Covers more complex concepts
------- fuâivla	copy-word	As brivla, but do not meet defining criteria of gismu or lujvo, ex: {angeli}	Covers unique concepts like names of places or organisms.
- cmavo
among these are:	grammar word. From âcmavlaâ, meaning âsmall wordâ	One consonant or less, ends in vowel.	Grammatical functions, varies.
-------- (many subcategories called selmaâo, with names like ZAhO and PU)			
Word-fragments:			
- rafsi	Affix.	3-5 letters, sometimes also a â â â. Begins with a consonant.	Never appears alone. Several rafsi form a lujvo.


cmevla are very easy to identify because they begin and end with a pause, signaled by a full stop in writing, and the last letter is a consonant. cmevla canât have any other function besides acting as a name. On the other hand, names which are not selbri cannot appear in Lojban without them being cmevla, or encased by certain quote words. One can mark stress in the names by capitalizing the letters which are stressed. Examples of cmevla are: {.iohAN.} (Johan, h is capital apostrophe), {.mat.} (Matt) and {.lutci.MIN.} (Lui-Chi Min). Names which does not end in consonants have to have one added: {.ivyn.} (Eve)

brivla are called âbridi-wordsâ because they by default are selbri, and therefore almost all Lojban words with a place structure are brivla. This has also given them the English nickname âcontent-wordsâ. Itâs nearly impossible to say anything useful without brivla, and almost all words for concepts outside lojban grammar are captured by brivla. As shown in the table, brivla has three subcategories:
gismu are the root words of the language. Only about 1450 exists, and very few new ones are added. They cover the most basic concepts like âcircleâ, âfriendâ, âtreeâ and âdreamâ. Examples include {zdani}, {pelxu} and {dunda}
lujvo are made by combining rafsi (see under rafsi), respresenting gismu. By combining rafsi, one narrows down the meaning of the word. lujvo are made by an elaborate algorithm, so making valid lujvo on the fly is near impossible, with few exceptions like {selpaâi}, from {se prami}, which can only have one definition. Instead, lujvo are made once, itâs place structure defined, and then that definition is made official by the dictionary. Examples include {brivla} (bridi-word), {cinjikca} (sexual-socializing = flirting) and {cakcinki} (shell-insect = beetle).
fuâivla are made by making up words which fit the definition for brivla, but not for lujvo or gismu. They tend to cover concepts which itâs hard to cover by lujvo, for instance names of species, nations or very cultural specific concepts. Examples include {gugdrgogurio} (Korea) {cidjrpitsa} (pizza) or {angeli} (angel).

cmavo are small words with one or zero consonants. They tend to not signify anything in the exterior world, but to have only grammatical function. Exceptions occur, and itâs debatable how much attitudinals exists for their grammatical function. If you have been paying attention, you would already be familiar with {du}, one of the few cmavo with a place structure. It is valid to type several cmavo in a row as one word, but in these lessons, that wonât be done. By grouping certain cmavo in functional units, though, it is sometimes easier to read. Thus, {.uipuzuvukumi citka} is valid for {.ui pu zu vu ku mi citka}. Like other Lojban words, one should (but need not always) place a full stop before any words beginning with a vowel.
cmavo of the form CVâVV or VâVV are experimental, and are words which are not in the formal grammar, but which have been added by Lojban users to respond to a certain need.

rafsi are not Lojban words, and can never appear alone. However, several (more than one) rafsi combine to form lujvo. These must still live up to the lujvo definition, for instance {lojban} is invalid because it ends in a consonant (which makes it a cmevla), and {ciâekei} is invalid because it does not contain a consonant cluster, and is thus read as two cmavo written as one word. Often, a 3-4 letter string is both a cmavo and a rafsi, like {zuâe}, which is both the BAI and the rafsi for {zukte}. Note that there is nowhere that both a cmavo and a rafsi would be grammatical, so these are not considered homophones. All gismu can double as rafsi, if they are prefixed with another rafsi. The first four letter of a gismu + y can also act as a rafsi, if they are suffixed. The vowel y can only appear in lujvo or cmevla. Valid rafsi letter combinations are: CVV, CVâV, CCV, CVCCy- CCVCy-, -CVCCV and -CCVCV.

Using what you know now, you should be able to answer the test i thus present:
Categorize each of the following words as cmevla (C), gismu (g), lujvo (l), fuâivla (f) or cmavo (c):
A) jai        G) mumbl
B) .irci        H) .iâi
C) bostu        I) cu
D) xelman        J) plajva
